The Wars That Changed Shape

Washington stopped bombing Iran and called it peace. In Abu Dhabi it stopped demanding a ceasefire and called it architecture. The instruments that survived need no one's permission, and the market has priced the renaming. The physical world has not.

By Josh Pilcher · Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Scroll

On Monday afternoon the President of the United States stood in the White House, fresh from a meeting with the prime minister of Qatar, and announced that the war with Iran was, militarily, effectively over. Almost nothing about the war had ended. The naval blockade of Iranian ports stays. The strait Iran closed in February stays closed to any ship Tehran has not approved. The day before the announcement, American forces fired on a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman and disabled it. What ended was the bombing, and what replaced it has a name of its own now: a task force of about twenty people in Tampa, created three days earlier, whose job is to strangle Iran by land because the sea blockade alone leaks.

Nine time zones away, in Abu Dhabi, three delegations sat down on Tuesday morning to talk about a different war. It was the first time Russians, Ukrainians and Americans had met in the same room since February. Europe, whose security is the stated subject of the talks, was in the building and not in the room. Russia's foreign minister helpfully explained the order of business: first a new security architecture for the whole continent, then, maybe, a ceasefire. Ukraine's position is the reverse. Between those two sentences sits the entire negotiation.

This report has one argument, and it runs from the Gulf to Abu Dhabi to Austin. Washington is converting two wars it cannot finish into instruments it can hold indefinitely: a blockade instead of a bombing campaign, a framework instead of a settlement. Both instruments share a property that matters more than any battlefield fact. Neither needs the permission of the Congress that voters elected on November 3 and that takes its seats on January 3. The market has already priced the conversion as peace. Brent crude has fallen about 22 percent from its October peak. The physical world, the insurance market, the diesel crack, the tanker count, has not agreed. And in Texas, the same trick is being played with a different commodity: a queue of power requests that exists mostly on paper is being governed as if it were real load, by a departing Republican governor's letters and an incoming Democratic governor's pledge, while the audit that decides how much of it is real lands on December 10.

The Bottom Line

Two wars changed shape this week; neither ended. In the Gulf, the United States stopped major strikes on Iran and kept everything that makes the war a war: a naval blockade now in its second life since July, a closed strait moving about a fifth of its normal traffic, and a new land blockade effort run by twenty staff in Tampa. In Abu Dhabi, the first Ukraine talks since February opened with Russia demanding that Europe's whole security order be renegotiated before any ceasefire, Europe itself outside the room, and the American secretary of state on record saying no concrete guarantee plan exists. Oil fell anyway, from an intraday high of $118 a barrel on October 30 to below $90 intraday on Tuesday, because markets price announcements and the announcement was peace. Underneath the price, the war is still being charged by the barrel: war risk insurance quoted at 6 to 10 percent of a ship's value in October, a diesel crack near $90, and Gulf exports still capped below their September level. At home, the bill for all of it arrived in one week: voters took both chambers of Congress from the President's party, October inflation printed hot again on Tuesday morning, and the Federal Reserve is now priced to raise rates in December, possibly by more than a quarter point. Houston and Texas are living their own version of the same story, a new county judge, a mayor redrawing police policy off an election he was not in, and a 474 gigawatt power queue that is mostly paper, waiting on a December audit to find out how much of it exists.

Chapter One

Abu Dhabi: the room, and who is not in it

The talks that opened Tuesday are the fourth round of a format that has so far produced prisoner exchanges and adjectives. The first three rounds, two in Abu Dhabi in January and February and one in Geneva on February 17 and 18, ended without progress on territory. Then the track went dark for nine months, and the reason matters: on February 28 the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, and the Ukraine file was shelved to make room for it. The two wars in this report are not parallel stories. One displaced the other, and it is only resuming now because the second war has been declared, by one side, to be over.

Russia's delegation tells you what Moscow thinks the meeting is for. Vladimir Medinsky leads it, as he has led Moscow's team since Istanbul in March 2022. Continuity of personnel is continuity of text. But this time he brought reinforcements with a specific meaning: Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, the head of military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, and a general staff operations officer, Yuri Zhigarlovsky. Ryabkov is the tell. He ran Russia's security guarantee talks with Washington in December 2021 and January 2022, the ones where Moscow demanded NATO roll back to its 1997 positions weeks before invading. His presence in Abu Dhabi means the file on the table is not a ceasefire line in Donetsk. It is the European order.

Sergei Lavrov said so out loud on Tuesday. Russia, he explained, cannot accept an immediate ceasefire without knowing what comes next, and finds it entirely reasonable to define the future security architecture of Europe first. A source in the Russian delegation put it more plainly to Reuters: the talks are about forming a new system of continental security, of which a Ukraine settlement is one part. Putin's aide Yury Ushakov has called for NATO to return to the positions it held before 1997, a demand that covers sixteen of the alliance's current members, including Poland, Finland and the Baltic states.

Ukraine's sequence is the mirror image. Ceasefire first, on the current line, then talk. Kyiv will not withdraw from land its army still holds, and the land at issue is not a leftover sliver. Russia controls about 80 percent of Donetsk, 79.7 percent on the DeepState map of October 30, and about a fifth of Ukraine overall. The fifth it does not hold in Donetsk is the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk fortress belt, fortified since 2014, which Russia has spent years failing to take by force. Moscow is asking at the table for the one thing its army could not take on the ground. That is not a residual detail to be tidied up on day two. It is the negotiation.

A guarantee Russia must approve is not a deterrent against Russia. It is a Russian veto written into Ukraine's defence.

Then there is the guarantee, the word doing the most work in Abu Dhabi and carrying the least content. Ukraine's demand dates to December 5, 1994, when it gave up the world's third largest nuclear arsenal under the Budapest Memorandum. The document said assurances, not guarantee. The signatories promised to respect Ukraine's borders and to consult if questions arose. Russia invaded anyway, twice. Kyiv's price ever since has been a mechanism, not a sentence: something modelled on NATO's Article 5, which itself commits allies only to take such action as each deems necessary. Washington has asked Moscow whether it would object to an Article 5-like guarantee for Ukraine, with the final decision reserved to President Trump personally. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was not in Abu Dhabi, said on Monday that the United States has not settled on a final concrete plan for what that guarantee would look like, and added that any guarantee has to be something Russia agrees to as well in order to work. Sit with that sentence. A guarantee Russia must approve is not a deterrent against Russia. It is a Russian veto written into Ukraine's defence. Day one lasted about four hours and produced the ritual vocabulary, constructive from Kyiv, very productive from Washington, plus talk of another large prisoner exchange. No text was published. No ceasefire language exists. The strikes, meanwhile, kept their own schedule: Russia hit ten Ukrainian regions overnight as the talks opened, struck five major electrical substations, and left six regions with outages. In the week to Tuesday, by President Zelenskyy's count, it was the heaviest air week of the year.

Europe's position in all this deserves its own paragraph, because Europe found a way to answer it the same day. The E4, Britain, France, Germany and Italy, plus NATO and the European Commission, met the American and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi before the trilateral session and were then left outside it, at Russia's insistence. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the format trilateral, full stop. Lavrov, asked about the Europeans in Abu Dhabi, suggested they could sit in a hotel there. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen answered that Europe's security can only be discussed after a ceasefire, with allies present. And on Tuesday in Oslo, ten northern nations, Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, signed a naval partnership aboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales, making the Joint Expeditionary Force NATO's maritime vanguard in the North Atlantic and the Baltic, with shared standards and a joint undersea surveillance effort to be operational within months. Read the two events together. In Abu Dhabi, Washington negotiates Europe's security with Russia while Europe waits outside. In Oslo, Europe builds a sea command of its own, British led, with Washington not in command. That is not a tantrum. It is a hedge, built by governments that have done the arithmetic on how much an American framework, agreed over their heads and needing their troops and money to mean anything, is actually worth.

Chapter Two

Hormuz: the war that kept its blockade

To understand what the President declared over on Monday, it helps to list what is still running. The naval blockade of Iranian ports, first imposed April 13, lifted June 18 under a memorandum of understanding, and reimposed July 14 after that memorandum collapsed, is in force. On November 7, American forces fired on the St. Kitts flagged cargo ship Huda in the Gulf of Oman and disabled it, the fifth vessel disabled since July; CENTCOM says 147 ships have been turned back in the same period and puts the Iranian crude kept off the market at more than $25 billion, a figure that comes from CENTCOM alone and whose method it has not published. The Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's petroleum moved before the war, is carrying roughly a fifth of its normal traffic. Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy has called it unsafe and closed since November 5 to any ship that does not coordinate with Tehran and use a Tehran approved route. The threat level set by the Joint Maritime Information Center remains severe. In October, 35 vessels were hit in and around the strait, the most in any month of the war, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre.

On top of this, on November 7, CENTCOM created Task Force Iron Gate. Its mission is to disrupt Iran's trade by land and through the Caspian Sea. Its strength is about twenty civilian and military personnel, based in Tampa, Florida. Iran has seven land neighbours and more than 5,000 kilometres of border. No agreement with Pakistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan or any other border state was announced with it. Twenty people cannot seal that frontier, and nobody serious claims otherwise. What Iron Gate actually is, is an admission: the sea blockade leaks, Washington knows it leaks, and the response is to formalise the leak hunt rather than to lift the blockade or finish the war. Tehran dismissed it as wordplay. The honest description is that both sides are now running blockades. Iran taxes and rations the strait. America taxes and rations Iran. Each calls the other's version an act of war and its own version a status quo.

Tehran's price for ending its half has not moved since September. Seven conditions, of which the core is simple: lift the blockade, release frozen assets, waive the oil sanctions, end the war on all fronts, and then Iran reopens the strait, in as little as two days, with nuclear talks after. Qatar is carrying a compressed version of that sequence, and its prime minister was in the Oval Office on Monday. But Iran's own officials spent the same two days denying that talks exist at all. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called reports of a meeting between the American vice president and Iran's security chief absolutely groundless. Mohsen Rezaei, who runs that security council's secretariat, told Washington to stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks. Rubio, for his part, said on Sunday that he does not see a deal coming soon and called some of Tehran's demands outrageous. The President says the other side is talking very politely. His secretary of state and their security chief both say, in public, that nothing is happening. Both cannot be the basis for policy, and the oil market, as we will see, chose the President's version anyway.

The market heard the word over. The strait did not.

The physical tells say what the strait thinks. Start with the price everyone watches, because it is the one that moved. January Brent touched $118 a barrel intraday on October 30, a six month high, and settled that day at $113.43. It settled at $98.32 on Friday, November 6. It settled at $92.57 on Monday, and on Tuesday it slipped below $90 for the first time since August 31 before settling, for January delivery, at $91.49. West Texas Intermediate settled at $86.04. Goldman Sachs, which tried to decompose the October rally on November 2, put the geopolitical premium at about $27 a barrel and fair value in the $90s. In other words, the entire fall is the premium leaving. The market has decided the shooting war is finished and has priced the barrel accordingly.

Now the tells that did not move. War risk insurance for a Hormuz transit, which cost about a quarter of one percent of a ship's value before the war, was quoted by brokers in October at 6 to 10 percent of hull value, up to $20 million for a single supertanker voyage. No November quote in the reporting shows it back anywhere near normal, and policies reprice every day or two, which means insurers are being paid, daily, to keep disbelieving the peace. Freight tells the same story. The cost of moving a barrel from the Gulf to East Asia on a very large crude carrier ran at roughly $36 to $37 a barrel in mid to late October, more than five times its pre-war level, on IEA reporting. A state linked fleet of tankers now carries much of what moves, because independent owners will not. Gulf exports, on Vortexa's count of crude, condensate and products from the region, averaged 17.1 million barrels a day in October, down from 18.9 million in September: oil is getting out, at about three quarters of its prewar rate, through bypass pipelines, ship to ship transfers in the dark, and Saudi Arabia's East West pipeline to the Red Sea. And the product market, the part that reaches a fuel tank, never got the peace memo at all. The diesel crack, the margin refiners earn turning crude into diesel, was about $90 a barrel in early November on EIA spot prices, and the Kansas City Fed noted on November 5 that diesel cracks are running at more than three times their year ago level and now account for more than 40 percent of the price of a gallon of diesel. Crude fell 22 percent. The price of turning crude into motion barely blinked.

Why can Saudi Arabia not simply open the taps and end the argument? Because the barrels are behind the gate. The International Energy Agency put Saudi production in September at 8.3 million barrels a day against sustainable capacity of 12.11 million. That looks like 3.8 million barrels of spare capacity until you ask how it leaves. With Hormuz rationed, the exportable route is one pipeline to the Red Sea, and the IEA's figure for spare capacity that can actually be brought to market within ninety days, for all of OPEC+, is 0.27 million barrels a day. The spare is in the well. The gate is insurance, one pipeline, and a strait run by the country the blockade is meant to punish. Meanwhile the buffer is spent: the chief executive of Abu Dhabi's national oil company said at the start of November that the conflict has drawn nearly a billion barrels out of global stockpiles. A price can fall on a press conference. It cannot refill a stockpile.

The clearest loser in this arrangement, among America's partners, is Qatar. It has no bypass pipeline. Its liquefied natural gas trains were damaged in March, its exports were halted, and in the first six months of the war it shipped 18 cargoes against 509 in the same period a year earlier, an estimated $24 billion in lost gas sales on Reuters calculations, with the cargo count from ICIS. That is why Qatar's prime minister was the man in the Oval Office on Monday, and why Qatar carries Tehran's paper. Mediation is what a country buys when its export route is held by both sides of a war. Saudi Arabia, by contrast, collects: every month the strait stays rationed justifies expanding the pipeline that routes around it, and Aramco is studying taking that line from 7 million barrels a day toward 10 million. A long blockade is bad for Riyadh's revenue and good for Riyadh's position, and position compounds.

Chapter Three

Washington: a mandate without gavels, a Fed without a choice

The midterm results were known on election night and they were not close in kind, whatever the final seat counts say. Democrats took both chambers of Congress. They hold at least 54 Senate seats, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled a week later, and a House majority whose final size is still being counted. They flipped seven Republican Senate seats and lost none of their own. They won the national House vote by about 13 points. The historical company for losing both chambers in one midterm is 1946, 1954, 1994 and 2006. For the margin, contemporaries reached for 1974.

What the voters were punishing is not a mystery, and the White House has stopped pretending otherwise. Exit polls put gasoline prices, the cost of living and the Iran war at the centre of the vote. A Reuters and Ipsos poll completed Monday, 1,705 adults, found the President's approval at 32 percent and 71 percent of Americans wanting the new Congress to pass legislation ending the Iran war, including 51 percent of Republicans. The Vice President's own post election assessment blamed the war. The President conceded the war was part of the reason his party lost. A war that costs a party both chambers is a war that gets renamed. That is the domestic fact underneath Monday's announcement, and underneath the speed of Abu Dhabi.

But a mandate is not a mechanism, and between now and January 3 there is no Democratic Congress, only a Democratic result. The outgoing Republican Congress still holds the gavels, and the calendar between here and Christmas is entirely its property. Government funding expires December 11. The Federal Reserve meets December 8 and 9. A White House panel's hearing into Fed Governor Lisa Cook, whom the President has tried to remove and whom the Supreme Court has so far protected, sits on December 14, moved there, her lawyer said, because she has to attend the Fed meeting first. Everything that will actually be decided this year is decided in that window, by people the voters have already fired or by a central bank they cannot fire at all. When the new Congress is seated, it will have subpoenas, committees, the power of the purse and a veto proof nothing. It cannot override a presidential veto. It cannot end a blockade by wishing. Its power over the wars is the power to make them expensive and investigated, which is real power, but it is slow power, and everyone at the tables in Abu Dhabi and Doha can read a calendar.

The Fed, meanwhile, delivered the week's most consequential number on Tuesday morning, and it was not the one the White House wanted. October's consumer price index rose 0.4 percent on the month, with core prices, excluding food and energy, up 0.3 percent for the third straight month. Both came in a tenth above forecast. There is no year over year figure for October, and there cannot be: the Bureau of Labor Statistics never collected October 2025 prices during last year's government shutdown, so the base month does not exist. Anyone quoting you an October inflation rate for the year is quoting a model. The last clean annual readings are September's: headline CPI up 3.7 percent, core up 2.6 percent, and the Fed's preferred measure, PCE, at 3.6 percent headline and 3.1 percent core. Around those sit a third quarter that grew at 3.4 percent annualised, October payrolls of 165,000 against about 65,000 expected, and unemployment at 4.1 percent. That is not an economy asking for relief. It is an economy giving its central bank cover to tighten.

Which it is doing. This hiking cycle is young and widely misremembered as a pause. The Fed raised rates on September 16, unanimously, the first increase since July 2023, under a chairman, Kevin Warsh, who was appointed by this President in the expectation of lower rates and took office in May saying he would deliver price stability, no ifs, ands or buts. On October 28 it held at 3.75 to 4.00 percent by ten votes to two, and both dissenters, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland's Beth Hammack, wanted a hike on the spot. What happened Tuesday turned a likely December hike into something close to a lock with a tail. Governor Christopher Waller, speaking in London before the print, said he favoured raising rates in December even if inflation cooled, and that a core reading of 0.3 percent or higher would put a half point move on the table. Core printed exactly 0.3 percent. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan then said at least two more quarter point hikes are clear. Market pricing after the release put about 85 percent on a quarter point in December and 11 to 15 percent on a half point, with a hold priced at almost nothing. Deutsche Bank's desk now expects hikes in December, January and March, taking the rate to 4.50 to 4.75 percent. The ten year Treasury closed Tuesday at 4.983 percent, having touched 5.31 percent in early October. The two year trades near 4.7 percent, above the top of the range the Fed is about to raise into. The front end is not forecasting the Fed. It is daring it.

The front end is not forecasting the Fed. It is daring it.

Notice what this does to the two wars. Cheaper crude was supposed to be Washington's reward for restraint, the disinflation that lets a central bank stand down. Instead the oil windfall arrived in the same week as a hot core print, so the Fed hikes anyway, the dollar stays strong, and the tightening gets exported to every government and company that borrows in dollars, Europe first among them. Europe enters winter with gas storage at about 75 percent against an original 90 percent target, euro area inflation at 4.0 percent in the October flash estimate, driven by energy, and its own central bank back to raising rates. The continent being negotiated over in Abu Dhabi is also the continent least able to pay for the guarantee it would have to provide. That is not a footnote to the talks. It is a reason the talks are structured to postpone the bill.

Chapter Four

China: a trillion dollars of leverage, pointed the other way

On the day the original trade truce with Washington was due to expire, Beijing published its customs figures for the first ten months of the year, and the number was built to be read in Washington. China's goods trade surplus reached $1.04 trillion, passing a trillion a month earlier than it did in 2025, on exports of $3.78 trillion. The day before, Beijing had announced a two month extension of the truce, to January 10, suspending its extra tariffs and its export control measures on American firms in two month slices it can renew or let lapse. A surplus announced on a deadline, by the side that controls the deadline's renewal, is not a statistic. It is an exhibit.

The exhibit needs reading carefully, because the headline flatters it in one direction and hides its meaning in another. The monthly surplus is narrowing, not widening: $105.3 billion in October, down from $133.5 billion in September, because imports grew faster than exports, up 41.6 percent against 35.2 percent. Those imports are not a Chinese consumer awakening. They are inputs: high tech goods up sharply, energy, copper, chips, bought to feed the export machine and to stockpile while a truce window is open. And the flagship export number, integrated circuits up 111.1 percent to $341.1 billion, is a value figure. The volume of chips shipped rose 3.2 percent. China is not shipping twice as many chips. It is selling into an artificial intelligence building boom at prices that have roughly doubled, while remaining a large net importer of the things themselves: chip imports were $566.5 billion over the same ten months, well above chip exports. Its bilateral surplus with the United States actually shrank slightly in October, to $32.7 billion. The largest part of the surplus is now with Europe, which is why European leaders, not American ones, are talking loudest about new barriers for 2027.

What the surplus is, then, is margin captured inside a broken supply chain, earned by the one major economy that can buy discounted energy, build the hardware the rest of the world is bidding for, and keep its own consumers quiet. It is real leverage, of a specific kind: Beijing arrives at the APEC summit in Shenzhen next week, where a third meeting this year between Presidents Xi and Trump is expected, holding a trillion dollar proof that its economy does not need American demand growth, a truce that expires in January under an incoming Congress that will scrutinise any concession, and a stockpile built at war prices that gets cheaper to refill at $90 oil. The vulnerability is equally specific. A genuine reopening of Hormuz would collapse the freight and insurance premiums embedded in the prices China charges and pays. An artificial intelligence spending correction would do the same to the chip values carrying its export growth. Analysts at Citi and Capital Economics are already flagging both base effects and momentum: on Capital Economics' seasonally adjusted reading, Chinese exports fell 2 percent in October from September. The trillion is a fact. What it will be worth in March is a bet.

Chapter Five

Houston: the election, cashed in within a week

Houston did not wait for January. Within seven days of the election, the city had a new balance of power at every level that touches it, and the mayor, who was not on any ballot, moved first.

Start at the county. Dr. Letitia Plummer defeated Orlando Sanchez for Harris County Judge by about 61 percent to 39 percent, on the largest midterm turnout in the county's history, 1.3 million voters. She succeeds Lina Hidalgo and becomes the first Black person and the first Muslim elected to the job, which in Texas is not a courtroom post: the county judge runs Commissioners Court, and with it the county budget, roads, flood control and public health. She earned that margin the hard way, beating former mayor Annise Parker in a runoff before beating the Republican in November. She inherits Hidalgo's court and its flood politics without inheriting Hidalgo's war with Austin, because Austin is changing hands too.

At City Hall, Mayor John Whitmire read the result on November 4, told his council that elections matter and relationships matter, and noted that his collaboration with the new state leadership had already begun. On Friday, November 6, he signed Executive Order 1-74, effective immediately, narrowing when Houston police may contact federal immigration authorities: only when a person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants and has a confirmed federal immigration warrant hit in the national database. Being suspected of an immigration violation, by itself, is no longer a basis for a call, a hold or a longer detention. The baseline it changes is small in count and large in signal: Houston police recorded 88 such database hits or contacts in the third quarter, out of 292,975 person checks, on the department's own October report. The legal ceiling is also clear. Texas Senate Bill 4, passed in 2017, bars local departments from limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities, and earlier this year the council retreated from a similar ordinance after the governor threatened to withhold more than $100 million in state funding. On November 9, three council members proposed writing the new limits into city code so a future mayor cannot undo them alone. The mayor's office replied that going further would put the city at even greater legal risk, and kept the order as an order. That exchange is the whole Houston story in miniature: a Democratic city testing, in real time, how much of the Abbott era's enforcement architecture simply expires on January 19, and how much of it is law that a new governor cannot repeal from a Republican Senate.

The city's own books carry a quieter fight. At the November 4 council meeting, the finance director reported August sales tax revenue of $76.2 million, up 5.7 percent on the year, and projected an ending fund balance of $351 million. The elected controller, Chris Hollins, told the same meeting his figure was $306 million. Forty five million dollars of disagreement between the mayor's team and the city's own watchdog, on the same ledger, in the year Houston most needs Austin and Washington to believe its numbers.

The Port, as usual, ignored the election and reported cargo. Port Houston handled 376,419 containers in September, up 11 percent on the year, with loaded imports up 16 percent, and 3.35 million containers through the first nine months, up 2 percent. Its executives announced in October that the port will study deepening the Ship Channel further, because its container terminals reach maximum capacity by 2033. The Port's constraints are federal, review and appropriations, and its clock is concrete: 2033 arrives regardless of who governs in Austin. What connects the Port to the rest of this report is what it carries. Houston is an export and resin port with a growing Asian import book, sitting downstream of two chokepoints: a Gulf freight market where moving crude to Asia cost more than five times its normal rate in October, and a trade truce with China that now expires on January 10, in front of a Congress elected partly on tariffs. Neither of those dates is set in Houston. Both of them are Houston dates.

And then there is power, where Houston's version of the paper problem lives. CenterPoint Energy raised its ten year capital plan by $4 billion on October 27, to $70.7 billion, on the expectation of 14 gigawatts of new demand through 2030. It has submitted 17 gigawatts to the state's large load process, about 10 gigawatts it calls base load and about 2 gigawatts studied, against a Houston system peak of about 21 gigawatts today. A regulated wires utility earns its return on what it builds, so every gigawatt that survives verification justifies substations and transmission lines, and CenterPoint is not a neutral forecaster of its own market. Whether its plan is a build or a press release depends on an audit in Austin that reports on December 10, which is where the Texas story takes over.

Chapter Six

Texas: a pledge, a pause, and a queue of paper

Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott on November 3, by roughly seven points on the Associated Press count. She will be Texas's first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor since Ann Richards left office in 1995. She takes office on January 19. Around her, the state flipped in pieces: Democrats swept the statewide executive offices and took the Texas House for the first time since 2003, Republicans held the Senate 19 to 12, and the lieutenant governor who will preside over that Republican Senate is a Democrat, Vikki Goodwin, whose real power will be whatever the Senate's own rules, adopted by its Republican majority in January, say it is. It is the state's first divided legislature in more than two decades.

The transition is being run from Houston. Its executive director is Joe Madden, a Houston native who was chief of staff to Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo. Its co chairs are a rural Republican former representative who fought school vouchers and the head of the state building trades council. That is not a victory lap staff. It is a coalition built for a Republican Senate and for construction delivery. Hinojosa's first stated personnel move tells the same story in reverse: she has pledged to fire the state education commissioner, Mike Morath, on day one. His term expires on January 10, nine days before she is sworn in. Even the firing is a negotiation with a calendar.

Her signature pledge is a moratorium on new data center approvals until the Legislature passes protections. It is a pledge, not a rule, and it lands on top of a pause that already exists and that her predecessor built out of letters. On August 3, Governor Abbott directed the grid operator, ERCOT, and the utility commission to audit every data center seeking a connection, and new energizations for large loads stopped. On September 21 he directed the environmental agency, TCEQ, to stop issuing data center permits until the audit finished. Those letters cite no statute, and the pause leaks: a report by FracTracker and Public Citizen in October counted 35 permitting actions on data center projects after the September directive, a claim the governor's office disputes. Construction already authorised continues. What the letters did accomplish, together with a rule the utility commission adopted on September 18, is to put a price on a rumour. A developer seeking a grid study for a load of 75 megawatts or more must now pay a $100,000 study fee and post financial security of $50,000 per megawatt of requested peak demand, $25 million for a 500 megawatt site, calculated on the full request with no discount for on site generation.

That price matters because the queue it prices is mostly paper. ERCOT's large load queue is quoted everywhere as about 474 gigawatts, more than five times the state's record peak demand of 91.1 gigawatts, set on July 22. As a count of requests it is real. As demand it is not. In ERCOT's April breakdown of a 445.8 gigawatt queue, 321 gigawatts had not submitted a single study. About 9 gigawatts had been approved to energize, on ERCOT's March count. Most of the queue was filed when filing was nearly free, by developers filing the same project in several places, which the new rules now force them to disclose under oath. The honest market number is narrower: Jefferies puts 13.3 gigawatts of announced Texas projects at risk from the new politics. The queue is a filing cabinet that learned to call itself a forecast.

The queue is a filing cabinet that learned to call itself a forecast.

December 10 is when the state starts emptying the cabinet. ERCOT files two reports with the utility commission that day, a verification of which projects in the first batch are real, and a community impact report on power, water, tax breaks and ownership, covering about 300 large projects. The early returns explain why the date matters. ERCOT surveyed 465 large loads and got answers from 93 percent, but it is having to send second round questions to about 80 percent of developers, on exactly the gaps that separate a project from a filing: site control, affiliate paperwork, equipment orders, security posted. The commission meets December 17 to consider exceptions, with Abbott still in the governor's chair and holding the pen on whether his own pause extends, narrows or lapses. A separate fight concludes December 31, over who pays for the transmission all of this would need. That one, not the moratorium, is the durable argument, because it decides what a surviving gigawatt costs the households around it.

The politics are unusually aligned, which is why the outcome is unusually hard to move. A University of Houston poll of 2,000 likely voters in October found 79 percent supporting limits on how many data centers get built, and 99 percent saying the projects should pay for the grid expansion they require. On the first day of bill filing, November 9, lawmakers filed 1,262 bills, and among the first was a Republican senator from Houston, Joan Huffman, proposing to repeal the data center sales tax exemption, which cost the state $1.02 billion in fiscal 2025 and $1.31 billion in fiscal 2026 on the Comptroller's figures. When the governor elect, the Republican Senate and 99 percent of the polled public agree on the direction, the fight is not about whether limits come. It is about grandfathering: which of the 138 certified projects keep their breaks, which filings die in December, and who writes the statute in a session where the House speaker, if Houston's Senfronia Thompson holds the 90 supporters she announced on November 6, including eight Republicans, will be a Houston Democrat governing by a coalition margin. Above the whole argument sits a state attorney general, Ken Paxton, who lost a Senate race last week and remains in office until January, with a live investigation into water compliance at 156 data center projects and a pending opinion on whether counties may impose moratoriums of their own. Harris County, which has 46 operating data centers and no zoning power at all, is waiting on that opinion to learn whether it is a player or a spectator.

Two closing facts keep the Texas story honest. The generators are fine. Vistra, the state's largest power producer, reported third quarter Texas earnings of $1.227 billion, 51.6 percent of its total and up 57 percent on the year, and had hedged about 98 percent of its expected 2027 generation by the end of October. Scarcity paid Vistra more this year than data center growth ever promised to. And the state budget is fine, for now: oil and gas production taxes brought in $8.3 billion in fiscal 2026, sales tax is running strong, and the Comptroller's revenue estimate for next year assumes oil at $66 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate at $86 is a margin cut for producers whose new well breakeven, on the Dallas Fed's 2026 breakeven survey, sits near $66. It is not a solvency event for the Permian, and it is not a revenue hole for Austin. What $86 oil plus a closed strait does squeeze is the margin in between: the freight on every barrel Houston ships to Asia, which is set not by the crude price but by the war the crude price has stopped believing in.

Chapter Seven

Two rival reads

Everything above supports two coherent readings of the same evidence. They differ on one question: whether instruments built to be sustainable, a blockade, a framework, a pause, can hold their value when the physical facts underneath them refuse to cooperate.

Read One

Read one: the renaming holds. On this read, Washington has found the stable form of both wars. A blockade costs no pilots, needs no new authorisation, and gets cheaper to sustain at home every week oil stays near $90. A framework process keeps Washington in the chair, keeps Moscow talking about Europe's order in a room Washington controls, and asks nothing of a Congress that has not been seated. Russia needs revenue and time more than it needs the fortress belt this winter. Iran's gate decays as bypass pipelines, dark transfers and a state tanker fleet learn to move oil around it, and as its own export earnings stay frozen. The Fed hikes in December, growth absorbs it, and the whole structure survives to be negotiated from strength in the spring. In Texas, the same logic applies: the pause becomes a permanent repricing of paper power through rules that outlive both governors. What would prove this read: a second day in Abu Dhabi that produces a written framework, signed or initialled, with Europeans inside the formal process; Hormuz flows and insurance improving together through November rather than price alone; a December rate hike that the bond market absorbs without the ten year breaking its October high; and a December 10 audit that cuts the Texas queue deeply and is then extended past inauguration day by agreement rather than by lapse.

Read Two

Read two: the paper breaks. On this read, the gap between the announced world and the physical one is the story, and gaps like that close suddenly. Brent near $90 has no war premium left in it, which means the next serious incident in the strait, in a month when 35 ships were hit, reprices the barrel by $15 to $27 in days, straight into a Federal Reserve that has just committed itself in public to considering a half point hike, with the two year yield already daring it to follow through. Abu Dhabi produces adjectives, Europe declines to fund or man a guarantee it did not negotiate, Kyiv declines to trade the fortress belt for an assurance modelled on the one that failed in 1994, and the framework is revealed as a process for postponing that refusal past January 3. In Texas, the pause lapses or is litigated, the audit disappoints everyone by re-asking questions instead of answering them, and the queue refills the moment filing looks cheap again. What would prove this read: another tanker incident cluster while Brent sits in the $80s; war risk quotes staying in their October range into December; no joint text out of Abu Dhabi on November 11 and public European refusal to underwrite one later; a December meeting that hikes by a half point or signals a faster path and pushes the ten year through 5.31 percent; and a December 17 utility commission meeting that lets the Texas pause lapse with no successor rule.

The difference between the reads is not optimism. It is where each one thinks reality is registered: in announcements, or in insurance quotes, substations and signed texts. This report's evidence sits mostly in the second register, which is why its bottom line is a warning rather than a celebration. But read one is not a fantasy. Blockades and frameworks have held for years at a time in other decades, precisely because they ask so little of the governments that run them. The deciding evidence arrives in the next five weeks, and most of it arrives in December.

Chapter Eight

Watchlist

  • 1November 11, Abu Dhabi, day two. A published joint text with a ceasefire line, a date and a named enforcer would break this report's scepticism. Adjectives, a prisoner exchange and a date for another round would confirm it. Watch also whether any European signs anything, rather than coordinating from the corridor.
  • 2November 18 and 25, the Fed's paper trail. The October meeting minutes on the 18th show whether the two hawkish dissenters were a wing or a majority in waiting. October PCE on the 25th is the last inflation print the Fed sees before it votes: core at 0.3 percent again locks the December hike and fattens the half point tail.
  • 3December 8 to 14, the Washington week. The Fed decides on the 9th, government funding expires on the 11th in a lame duck session, November inflation prints on the 10th, one day too late to matter, and the Cook hearing lands on the 14th. A hike, a funding fight and a central bank independence fight inside six days, all before the elected Congress exists.
  • 4December 10 and 17, the Texas filter. ERCOT's verification and community impact reports on the 10th, then the utility commission on the 17th, with Abbott still holding the pen. The share of the queue disqualified is the single most informative number in Texas energy this year, and the December 31 ruling on who pays for transmission is the one that lasts.
  • 5January 3 to 19, the handover stack. The new Congress is seated January 3, the American Chinese trade truce expires January 10, the Texas Legislature convenes and elects a speaker on January 12, and Governor Hinojosa is sworn in on January 19. Every instrument described in this report was designed to survive exactly this stack. Whether it does is the next report.
